claim: Parkinson's disease (PD) affects 0.3% of the general population, with a majority of cases being sporadic.
source: Parkinson's disease (PD) affects 0.3% of the general population, with a majority of cases being sporadic (Obeso, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Obeso, 2017

claim: The hallmark of PD is a selective vulnerability of substantia nigra dopamine (DA) neurons.
source: The hallmark of PD is a selective vulnerability of substantia nigra dopamine (DA) neurons among others (Gonzalez-Rodriguez et al., 2020), accompanied by both motor and non-motor features, as well as prominent Lewy body pathology and mitochondrial dysfunction (Bose and Beal, 2016; Tarakad and Jankovic, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gonzalez-Rodriguez et al., 2020

claim: PD is accompanied by both motor and non-motor features, as well as prominent Lewy body pathology and mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: The hallmark of PD is a selective vulnerability of substantia nigra dopamine (DA) neurons among others (Gonzalez-Rodriguez et al., 2020), accompanied by both motor and non-motor features, as well as prominent Lewy body pathology and mitochondrial dysfunction (Bose and Beal, 2016; Tarakad and Jankovic, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bose and Beal, 2016; Tarakad and Jankovic, 2020

claim: The economic cost of PD is estimated to be at least $51.9 billion a year in the United States.
source: As one of the world's fastest growing neurological disorders, the economic cost of PD is estimated to be at least $51.9 billion a year in the United States (Yang, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang, 2020

claim: Current drug therapies for PD provide only symptomatic relief by enhancing dopaminergic action, decreasing metabolism of DA, or replacing the natural form of DA with exogenous drugs.
source: The current drug therapies available for PD provide only symptomatic relief by enhancing the dopaminergic action, decreasing metabolism of DA, or replacing the natural form of DA with exogenous drugs (Haddad et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Haddad et al., 2017

claim: Chronic levodopa therapy can result in motor fluctuation and dyskinesia.
source: While it provides benefits in improving motor symptoms in the short term, chronic therapy can result in motor fluctuation and dyskinesia.

claim: Many PD patients experience a wearing-off effect where levodopa loses its efficacy even with dosing adjustments.
source: Furthermore, many patients experience a wearing-off effect where levodopa loses its efficacy even with dosing adjustments.
evidence: Stated as established clinical observation

claim: There is yet to be a therapy that can halt or slow down PD disease progression.
source: Despite potentially promising efforts (Dawson and Dawson, 2019), there is yet to be a therapy that can halt or slow down disease progression.
evidence: Stated as current state of the field with citation to Dawson and Dawson, 2019

claim: The phase I to approval rate for neurological diseases was only 8.4% from 2006 to 2015.
source: In recent years, the drug discovery pipeline for neurological diseases has been stagnant, with a phase I to approval rate being only 8.4% from 2006 to 2015 (Wong et al., 2019) which is lower than the average approval rate of all therapeutic indications.
evidence: Supported by citation to Wong et al., 2019

claim: The phase I to approval rate for neurological diseases is lower than the average approval rate of all therapeutic indications.
source: In recent years, the drug discovery pipeline for neurological diseases has been stagnant, with a phase I to approval rate being only 8.4% from 2006 to 2015 (Wong et al., 2019) which is lower than the average approval rate of all therapeutic indications.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of neurological disease approval rate to all therapeutic indications

claim: The lack of success in neurological drug discovery can be attributed to the difficulty of target-based drug discovery in the setting of neurological diseases because of complex etiology and biological pathways.
source: One of the reasons for such lack of success can be attributed to the fact that conventional approach of target-based drug discovery is difficult in the setting of neurological diseases because of the complex etiology and biological pathways involved.
evidence: Stated as reasoning based on established understanding

claim: Phenotypic screening provides a promising opportunity for drug discovery in neurological diseases.
source: Phenotypic screening provides a promising opportunity.

claim: Whole organism-based drug discovery has been successfully applied to model organisms.

claim: Larval zebrafish offer multiple advantages for drug screening including genomic and anatomical conservation and high throughput capabilities.

claim: Zebrafish screens have uncovered therapeutic leads that are currently in clinical testing and/or shed light on biological mechanisms.

claim: The NTR-MTZ chemogenetic DA neuron ablation model in larval zebrafish shows robust DA neuronal loss 24 hours after adding MTZ to 5 days post fertilization larvae.
source: Twenty-four hours (hrs) after adding MTZ to 5 days post fertilization (dpf) larval zebrafish, we observed at 6 dpf robust DA neuronal loss in the ventral forebrain region (Figure 1A), the homologous group to mammalian substantia nigDA (Rink and Wullimann, 2001).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and citation to Rink and Wullimann, 2001 for anatomical homology

claim: The ventral forebrain DA neurons in zebrafish are homologous to mammalian substantia nigra DA neurons.

evidence: Supported by citation to Rink and Wullimann, 2001

claim: MTZ treatment causes significant damage to mitochondrial DNA but not nuclear DNA in DA neurons.
source: This data uncovered a significant damage of mitochondrial DNA but not nuclear DNA in MTZ-exposed individuals (Figure 1B).

claim: Mitochondrial DNA damage occurs 8 hours after MTZ treatment, when DA neurons remain morphologically intact.
source: Total DNAs were extracted from DA neurons in DMSO control and 4.5 mM MTZ-treated transgenic larvae (8 hr after MTZ treatment, when DA neurons remain morphologically intact).
evidence: Stated as observation from experimental procedure

claim: Nuclear DNA is unaffected by MTZ possibly due to protection by nucleosomes.
source: The nuclear DNA was unaffected possibly due to protection by nucleosomes; this observation also supports the notion that the time of our DNA integrity assessment precedes that of overt neurodegeneration.
evidence: Stated as speculation based on experimental observation

claim: MTZ treatment causes reduced mitochondrial number in DA neurons.
source: We next performed in vivo time-lapse imaging, which uncovered mitochondrial dysfunction in morphologically intact DA neurons after MTZ treatment. These include reduced mitochondrial number, increased mitochondrial length, decreased motility and velocity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from live imaging shown in Figure 1C-H

claim: MTZ treatment causes increased mitochondrial length in DA neurons.
source: We next performed in vivo time-lapse imaging, which uncovered mitochondrial dysfunction in morphologically intact DA neurons after MTZ treatment. These include reduced mitochondrial number, increased mitochondrial length, decreased motility and velocity.

claim: MTZ treatment causes decreased mitochondrial velocity in DA neurons.

claim: In MTZ-treated DA neurons, mobile mitochondria move exclusively in retrograde direction toward neuronal soma.
source: Interestingly, in MTZ-treated DA neurons, mobile mitochondria moved exclusively in retrograde direction toward neuronal soma, suggesting that they are targeted for repair and/or mitophagy (Figure 1C–H; Figure 1—videos 1; 2).

claim: Retrograde movement of mitochondria in MTZ-treated DA neurons suggests they are targeted for repair and/or mitophagy.
source: Interestingly, in MTZ-treated DA neurons, mobile mitochondria moved exclusively in retrograde direction toward neuronal soma, suggesting that they are targeted for repair and/or mitophagy (Figure 1C–H; Figure 1—videos 1; 2).

claim: Mitochondrial defects are observed prior to DA neurodegeneration in the NTR-MTZ model.
source: Together, mitochondrial defects are observed prior to DA neurodegeneration in the NTR-MTZ model, suggesting that mitochondrial DNA damage and ensuing mitochondrial dysfunction is likely a cause rather than a consequence of DA neuron degeneration.

claim: Mitochondrial DNA damage and ensuing mitochondrial dysfunction is likely a cause rather than a consequence of DA neuron degeneration in the NTR-MTZ model.

claim: Increased expression of pink1 is neuroprotective in the NTR-MTZ model.

claim: CBE exhibits some selectivity for GBA1 but can also inhibit lysosomal α-glucosidase (GAA), non-lysosomal glucosylceramidase (GBA2), and lysosomal β-glucuronidase (GUSB).
source: CBE exhibits some selectivity for GBA1 but can also inhibit lysosomal α-glucosidase (GAA), non-lysosomal glucosylceramidase (GBA2), and lysosomal β-glucuronidase (GUSB).
evidence: Stated as known property of CBE

claim: CBE dose-dependently reduces DA neuron integrity and locomotor activity in larval zebrafish, with 500 μM yielding significant results.
source: We first observed that CBE dose-dependently reduced DA neuron integrity and locomotor activity in larval zebrafish, with 500 μM in the medium yielding significant results (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Both levodopa and olmesartan ameliorate locomotor deficits induced by CBE.
source: While both levodopa and olmesartan ameliorated locomotor deficits induced by CBE (Figure 4A–B), only olmesartan rescued TH immunoreactivity deficits induced by CBE treatment (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-B

claim: Only olmesartan rescues TH immunoreactivity deficits induced by CBE treatment.
source: While both levodopa and olmesartan ameliorated locomotor deficits induced by CBE (Figure 4A–B), only olmesartan rescued TH immunoreactivity deficits induced by CBE treatment (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C-D

claim: CBE preferentially damages TH neurons as revealed by double immunofluorescent staining of TH and 5HT.
source: Furthermore, CBE preferentially damaged TH neurons as revealed by the double immunofluorescent staining of TH and 5HT (serotonin) (Figure 4C and E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and E

claim: Olmesartan and captopril treatment significantly protect against MPP+-induced DA neuronal loss.
source: Imaging of ventral forebrain DA neurons showed that MPP+ treatment significantly reduced DA neuron intensity, and treatment with Olmesartan and captopril significantly protected against DA neuronal loss (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: RAAS inhibitors are neuroprotective in a Gaucher disease model and a MPP+ model.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that RAAS inhibitors are not only neuroprotective in the synthetic NTR-MTZ model but is also neuroprotective in a Gaucher disease model and a MPP+ model.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments in multiple models

claim: The findings in the Gaucher disease and MPP+ models reinforce the validity of the NTR-MTZ synthetic model for neuroprotective small molecule screening.
source: These findings reinforce the validity of the NTR-MTZ synthetic model for neuroprotective small molecule screening.
evidence: Inference based on consistency of results across multiple models

claim: The two neurotoxic models (MTZ and CBE) share significant overlap in gene expression changes and form distinct clusters compared to control groups.
source: Upon annotating the sequence reads with the GRCz11 genome assembly, normalizing the read counts, and plotting all the significant gene expression changes (α = 0.05, FDR = 0.1)(Figure 5—figure supplement 1), we noted that the two neurotoxic models shared significant overlap and formed distinct clusters compared to the DMSO- or olmesartan alone control groups.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Treatment of both neurotoxic models with olmesartan restores transcriptomic expression to levels similar to controls.
source: Furthermore, treatment of both neurotoxic models with olmesartan restored transcriptomic expression to levels that were similar to controls, especially on the transcriptomes up regulated in the neurotoxic models (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: The expression of 1248 genes were commonly altered in the two neurotoxic models compared to vehicle controls.
source: The expression of 1248 genes were commonly altered in the two neurotoxic models compared to vehicle controls (Figure 5C), while the expression of 507 genes were commonly altered by olmesartan co-treatment in comparison to each of the neurotoxic insult alone (α = 0.05, FDR = 0.1) (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5C

claim: The expression of 507 genes were commonly altered by olmesartan co-treatment in comparison to each of the neurotoxic insult alone.
source: The expression of 1248 genes were commonly altered in the two neurotoxic models compared to vehicle controls (Figure 5C), while the expression of 507 genes were commonly altered by olmesartan co-treatment in comparison to each of the neurotoxic insult alone (α = 0.05, FDR = 0.1) (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5D

claim: The expression of RAAS pathway genes prorenin receptor (PRR), agtr1b, and ace2 were significantly upregulated in the MTZ treated group compared to control.
source: The expression of RAAS pathway genes prorenin receptor (PRR, gene name atp6ap2), agtr1b, and ace2 were significantly upregulated in the MTZ treated group compared to the control (padj = 0.001, 0.032, and 0.015 respectively).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis

claim: The atp6ap2 gene was significantly upregulated in the CBE-treated group compared to control.
source: The atp6ap2 was also significantly upregulated in the CBE-treated group compared to the control (padj <0.001).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis

claim: Pathway enrichment analysis showed 28 significantly altered pathways in the neurotoxic models when compared to vehicle controls.
source: Pathway enrichment analysis with the Reactome and KEGG pathway database showed 28 significantly altered pathways in the neurotoxic models when compared to vehicle controls (p < 0.01).
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data

claim: The differentially expressed genes common to both neurotoxic models show high significance for the PD KEGG pathway.
source: Interestingly, the differentially expressed genes common to both neurotoxic models showed high significance (LogP = –2.55) for the PD KEGG pathway (ID: hsa05012).
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data

claim: The neurotoxic models used in this study are relevant to PD.
source: These results further reinforce the notion that the neurotoxic models used in this study are relevant to PD.
evidence: Inference based on pathway enrichment analysis showing PD pathway significance

claim: Several pathways related to mitochondrial function such as ATP synthesis, oxidative stress, and electron transport chain show the highest significance values in the neurotoxic models.
source: Cluster analysis of the gene ontology and pathways using g:Profiler, DAVID (version 6.8)(Huang et al., 2009), and Metascape (Zhou, 2019) GO enrichment revealed distinct ontology clusters that were altered in both neurotoxic models compared to controls. Importantly, several pathways related to the mitochondrial function such as ATP synthesis, oxidative stress, and electron transport chain showed the highest significance values (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5E

claim: Olmesartan treatment significantly affects clusters related to mitochondrial function including respiratory electron transport, oxidative phosphorylation, ATP metabolic process, and inorganic cation transport.
source: Olmesartan treatment, when compared to the neurotoxic models, significantly affected the clusters related to mitochondrial function, including respiratory electron transport, oxidative phosphorylation, ATP metabolic process, and inorganic cation transport, (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5F

claim: Preferential mitochondrial DNA damage is observed in DA neurons of the NTR-MTZ model prior to neuronal loss.
source: As described earlier, preferential mitochondrial DNA damage was observed in DA neurons of the NTR-MTZ model prior to neuronal loss (Figure 1B).
evidence: Reference to earlier experimental result shown in Figure 1B

claim: There is a strong link between mitochondrial dysfunction and lysosomal storage diseases.
source: There is also a strong link to mitochondrial dysfunction in lysosomal storage diseases (Plotegher and Duchen, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Plotegher and Duchen, 2017

claim: Disruption of mitochondrial gene expression is possibly causal to DA neuron degeneration in the neurotoxic models.
source: Thus, disruption of mitochondrial gene expression is possibly causal to DA neuron degeneration in these models.
evidence: Inference based on temporal sequence and pathway analysis

claim: Fourteen genes that were significantly up-regulated in the neurotoxic models behave oppositely upon olmesartan treatment.
source: Fourteen genes that were significantly up regulated in the neurotoxic models behaved oppositely upon olmesartan treatment (genes highlighted in blue in Table 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Table 1

claim: The fourteen genes that are oppositely regulated by olmesartan function in the mitochondrial electron transport chain and TOM-TIM complex.
source: They function in the mitochondrial electron transport chain (e.g. Complex I, III, IV, and V) and TOM-TIM complex critical for protein translocation through the mitochondrial membrane.
evidence: Functional annotation of genes identified in RNA-seq analysis

claim: Trim3, which was significantly down-regulated in the neurotoxic models, was up-regulated by olmesartan co-treatment.
source: One gene, trim3, which was significantly down-regulated in the neurotoxic models, was up-regulated by olmesartan co-treatment (highlighted in red in Table 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Table 1

claim: Trim3 is found to be down-regulated in PD patient plasma.
source: Trim3 (Tripartite motif containing 3), with reported ubiquitin ligase activity, is found to be down-regulated in PD patient plasma (Dong, 2019) and can attenuate apoptosis via activating PI3K/AKT signaling pathway in PD models (Dong, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dong, 2019

claim: Trim3 can attenuate apoptosis via activating PI3K/AKT signaling pathway in PD models.
source: Trim3 (Tripartite motif containing 3), with reported ubiquitin ligase activity, is found to be down-regulated in PD patient plasma (Dong, 2019) and can attenuate apoptosis via activating PI3K/AKT signaling pathway in PD models (Dong, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dong, 2020

claim: Many mitochondrial pathways are no longer significantly altered when comparing olmesartan+CBE or olmesartan+MTZ groups to vehicle control.
source: Many of these mitochondrial pathways were no longer significantly altered when comparing the olmesartan+ CBE or olmesartan+ MTZ groups to the vehicle control group (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis in Supplementary file 1

claim: Active AGTR1 receptor is necessary for upregulating the expression of mitochondrial electron transport pathway genes in both neurotoxic models.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that active AGTR1 receptor is necessary for upregulating the expression of mitochondrial electron transport pathway genes and downregulating trim3 in both neurotoxic models.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from RNA-seq analysis showing gene expression changes

claim: Active AGTR1 receptor is necessary for downregulating trim3 in both neurotoxic models.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that active AGTR1 receptor is necessary for upregulating the expression of mitochondrial electron transport pathway genes and downregulating trim3 in both neurotoxic models.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from RNA-seq analysis showing gene expression changes

claim: Inhibiting AGTR1 activity can help restore normalcy of mitochondrial pathways, leading to neuroprotection.
source: Inhibiting its activity can help restore normalcy of these pathways, leading to neuroprotection.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from RNA-seq and neuroprotection data

claim: Drosophila offers a plethora of genetic PD models in which DA neuronal loss is evident.
source: Drosophila offers a plethora of genetic PD models in which DA neuronal loss is evident (West et al., 2015; Lu and Vogel, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to West et al., 2015; Lu and Vogel, 2009

claim: The conserved PINK1-Parkin pathway that directs mitochondrial quality control has been originally delineated in flies.
source: The conserved PINK1-Parkin pathway that directs mitochondrial quality control (MQC) has been originally delineated in flies (Yang et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2003; Greene, 2003; Park, 2006; Clark, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yang et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2003; Greene, 2003; Park, 2006; Clark, 2006

claim: Drosophila PD models have been used in genetic and pharmacological testing for genes and agents that offer neuroprotection.
source: These models have been used in genetic and pharmacological testing for genes and agents that offer neuroprotection (Wang, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang, 2006

claim: Genes encoding angiotensin converting enzymes are detected in Drosophila.
source: Although the RAAS pathway similar to vertebrates has not been fully described in Drosophila, genes encoding the angiotensin converting enzymes are detected in this species (Coates, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Coates, 2000

claim: RAAS inhibitors rescue memory defects in a Drosophila Alzheimer's disease model.
source: Recently, it has also been reported that RAAS inhibitors rescue memory defects in a Drosophila Alzheimer's disease model (Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2020

claim: The Drosophila pink1 model recapitulates key features of PD including mitochondrial dysfunction, aberrant mitochondrial morphology, DA neuron and muscular degeneration.
source: We therefore tested olmesartan in the Drosophila pink1 model, which recapitulates key features of PD including mitochondrial dysfunction, aberrant mitochondrial morphology, DA neuron and muscular degeneration.
evidence: Stated as established characteristics of the Drosophila pink1 model

claim: The most robust phenotype of pink1 mutant flies is the degeneration of their indirect flight muscle caused by accumulation of dysfunctional and morphologically aberrant mitochondria.
source: The most robust phenotype of the pink1 mutant flies is the degeneration of their indirect flight muscle caused by the accumulation of dysfunctional and morphologically aberrant mitochondria.
evidence: Stated as established characteristic of the pink1 mutant phenotype

claim: Pink1 mutant flies have collapsed thorax (thoracic indentation) and abnormal wing posture.
source: This results in flies with collapsed thorax (thoracic indentation) and abnormal wing posture, manifested as droopy or held-up wings as opposed to the straight wings in control animals.
evidence: Stated as established characteristic of the pink1 mutant phenotype

claim: Treatment of pink1 mutant flies with 100 μM olmesartan results in significant rescue of wing posture.
source: Treatment of pink1 mutant flies by feeding them with food containing 100 μM olmesartan resulted in significant rescue of wing posture (Figure 6A–C) and the thoracic indentation (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A-C

claim: Treatment of pink1 mutant flies with 100 μM olmesartan results in significant rescue of thoracic indentation.
source: Treatment of pink1 mutant flies by feeding them with food containing 100 μM olmesartan resulted in significant rescue of wing posture (Figure 6A–C) and the thoracic indentation (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D-F

claim: Olmesartan rescues abnormal mitochondrial morphology in DA neurons of pink1 mutant flies.
source: The abnormal mitochondrial morphology and neuronal loss phenotypes in DA neurons were also rescued (Figure 6G–J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G-J

claim: Olmesartan rescues neuronal loss in DA neurons of pink1 mutant flies.
source: The abnormal mitochondrial morphology and neuronal loss phenotypes in DA neurons were also rescued (Figure 6G–J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G-J

claim: Olmesartan's protective effect is conserved across species.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that olmesartan's protective effect is conserved across species.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments in zebrafish and Drosophila

claim: The PPMI database includes a total of 423 de novo PD patients.
source: We used the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) database, which includes a total of 423 de novo PD patients, 308 of which had complete data (accurate medication and medical history records for each visit throughout the longitudinal study, no missing records on age, gender, duration of PD, and high visit compliance with no more than three missing records for motor assessment score).
evidence: Description of the PPMI database used for analysis

claim: 308 de novo PD patients in the PPMI database had complete data.
source: We used the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) database, which includes a total of 423 de novo PD patients, 308 of which had complete data (accurate medication and medical history records for each visit throughout the longitudinal study, no missing records on age, gender, duration of PD, and high visit compliance with no more than three missing records for motor assessment score).
evidence: Description of the PPMI database used for analysis

claim: De novo PD patients refer to subjects who have a diagnosis of PD for two years or less and are not taking any PD medications at the time of enrollment.
source: The de novo PD patients refer to subjects who have a diagnosis of PD for two years or less and are not taking any PD medications at the time of enrollment.
evidence: Definition provided for the patient cohort

claim: Among the 308 PD patients with complete data, 96 patients were on RAAS inhibitors while 212 patients were not.
source: Among them, 96 patients were on RAAS inhibitors (RAAS) while 212 patients were not (non-RAAS).
evidence: Description of patient cohort composition

claim: Among the non-RAAS cohort, 42 patients were hypertensive and taking other medications for hypertension management.
source: Among the non-RAAS cohort, 42 patients were hypertensive and taking other medications such as calcium channel blockers or diuretics for the management of hypertension (Figure 7A).
evidence: Description of patient cohort composition shown in Figure 7A

claim: Previous studies examining electronic health records reported mixed results regarding the effect of RAAS inhibitors on the incidence of PD.
source: Previous studies that interrogate electronic health records (EHR) data reported mixed results regarding the effect of RAAS inhibitors on the incidence of PD (Lee et al., 2014; Warda et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lee et al., 2014; Warda et al., 2019

claim: There are no accepted progression biomarkers for PD at present.
source: At present, there are no accepted progression biomarkers for PD (Espay et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Espay et al., 2017

claim: The UPDRS suffers from limitations including subjectivity and ambiguities in the written text.
source: The Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS), while widely utilized, suffers from limitations including subjectivity and ambiguities in the written text (Movement Disorder Society Task Force on Rating Scales for Parkinson's Disease, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Movement Disorder Society Task Force on Rating Scales for Parkinson's Disease, 2003

claim: Clinicians delay the prescription of levodopa to PD patients until absolutely necessary for treating debilitating motor symptoms because of wear-off and debilitating side effects after prolonged use.
source: Because of the wear-off and debilitating side effects of levodopa after prolonged use (Espay, 2018), clinicians delay the prescription of levodopa to PD patients until absolutely necessary for treating debilitating motor symptoms.
evidence: Stated as clinical practice with citation to Espay, 2018

claim: Patients on RAAS inhibitors have a significantly delayed onset of levodopa therapy compared to patients not on RAAS inhibitors.
source: After propensity score matching between RAAS and no-RAAS cohorts (Figure S8A-C), our analysis found that the patients on RAAS inhibitors had a significantly delayed onset of levodopa therapy compared to the patients not on RAAS inhibitors (difference, –5.8; 95% CI –11.26 to –0.4254; p = 0.035) (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by clinical data analysis shown in Figure 7B

claim: Patients on RAAS inhibitors have a significantly delayed onset of levodopa therapy compared to those on other classes of anti-hypertensive medications.
source: To control for hypertension as a variable, we compared patients on RAAS inhibitors to those on other classes of anti-hypertensive medications. This analysis also uncovered a significant effect of RAAS inhibitors in delaying the onset of levodopa therapy as shown in the Kaplan Meier curve (p = 0.032) (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by clinical data analysis shown in Figure 7C

claim: The UPDRS part I score shows a significantly lower score in the cohort on RAAS inhibitors compared to cohorts not on RAAS inhibitors or those taking other hypertensive medications over 5 years.
source: The UPDRS part I score, which examines the mentation, behavior, and mood, showed a significantly lower score in the cohort on RAAS inhibitors compared to the cohorts not on RAAS inhibitors or those taking other hypertensive medications over the course of 5 years (difference: NO RAAS vs RAAS = 0.289, Other HTN vs RAAS = 0.266, p = 0.017) (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by clinical data analysis shown in Figure 7D

claim: The UPDRS part 2 and part 3 do not show significance in patients taking RAAS inhibitors when compared to other cohorts.
source: The UPDRS part 2 and part 3, which examine the activities of daily living and motor function respectively, did not show significance in patients taking RAAS inhibitors when compared to other cohorts (p = 0.82) (Figure S8E-F).
evidence: Supported by clinical data analysis shown in Figure S8E-F

claim: Inhibition of RAAS signaling slows down disease progression in human PD patients.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that inhibition of RAAS signaling slows down disease progression in human PD patients.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from clinical data analysis

claim: The NTR-MTZ-based chemogenetic DA neuron ablation model in zebrafish is validated by showing that DA neuronal loss is preceded by preferential mitochondrial DNA damage and ensuing mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: Here, we validated the NTR-MTZ-based chemogenetic DA neuron ablation model in zebrafish by showing that DA neuronal loss is preceded by preferential mitochondrial DNA damage and ensuing mitochondrial dysfunction.
evidence: Summary of experimental validation results

claim: The study used the NTR-MTZ system to conduct a high-content DA neuron imaging-based chemical screen.
source: We then used this system to conduct a high-content DA neuron imaging-based chemical screen and identified the inhibitors of Renin-Angiotensin (RAAS) system to be significantly neuroprotective via cell-autonomous effects of the angiotensin receptor one in DA neurons.
evidence: Summary of experimental approach and findings

claim: RAAS inhibitors are significantly neuroprotective via cell-autonomous effects of angiotensin receptor 1 in DA neurons.
source: We then used this system to conduct a high-content DA neuron imaging-based chemical screen and identified the inhibitors of Renin-Angiotensin (RAAS) system to be significantly neuroprotective via cell-autonomous effects of the angiotensin receptor one in DA neurons.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: Dopamine neuron-specific RNA-seq reveals the molecular action of RAAS signaling in mitochondrial gene regulation.
source: Dopamine neuron-specific RNA-seq further revealed the molecular action of RAAS signaling in mitochondrial gene regulation.
evidence: Summary of RNA-seq findings

claim: Inhibition of RAAS signaling is neuroprotective across species.
source: Finally, inhibition of RAAS signaling was neuroprotective across species.
evidence: Summary of findings across zebrafish, Drosophila, and human studies

claim: This study identifies RAAS inhibitors as promising therapeutics for slowing down PD progression.
source: Together, this study identifies RAAS inhibitors as promising therapeutics for slowing down PD progression and highlights a new approach composed of high content screening in zebrafish, cross-species validation, and examination of human clinical data to uncover previously unrecognized neuroprotective agents and underlying mechanisms.
evidence: Overall conclusion of the study

claim: The study highlights a new approach composed of high content screening in zebrafish, cross-species validation, and examination of human clinical data to uncover neuroprotective agents.
source: Together, this study identifies RAAS inhibitors as promising therapeutics for slowing down PD progression and highlights a new approach composed of high content screening in zebrafish, cross-species validation, and examination of human clinical data to uncover previously unrecognized neuroprotective agents and underlying mechanisms.
evidence: Overall conclusion about the methodological approach

claim: The underlying mechanism of MTZ-mediated cell death in vertebrates has remained elusive.
source: Although MTZ has historically been widely prescribed as an antibiotic, the underlying mechanism of cell death in vertebrates has however remained elusive.
evidence: Stated as knowledge gap

claim: This study links the mode of NTR-MTZ-mediated cell death to mitochondrial dysfunction for the first time.
source: By investigating the integrity of mitochondrial and nuclear DNAs, performing live imaging of mitochondria, and DA neuron-specific RNA-seq, we link the mode of NTR-MTZ-mediated cell death to mitochondrial dysfunction for the first time to our knowledge.
evidence: Claim of novelty based on experimental findings

claim: The NTR-MTZ-mediated cell ablation model in larval zebrafish is a valuable small molecule discovery tool for disorders where mitochondrial dysfunction is a prevalent pathophysiological mechanism.
source: This property, together with its safe and scalable nature, makes the NTR-MTZ-mediated cell ablation model in larval zebrafish a valuable small molecule discovery tool for disorders where mitochondrial dysfunction is a prevalent underlying pathophysiological mechanism.
evidence: Conclusion about the utility of the model based on its characteristics

claim: The NTR-MTZ model has limitations including not being able to recapitulate the etiology of PD and the time course of neurodegeneration.
source: Despite the mechanistic relevance of the NTR-MTZ model to PD in the context of mitochondrial dysfunction, this model has several limitations, including not being able to recapitulate the etiology of PD and the time course of neurodegeneration.
evidence: Acknowledgment of model limitations

claim: Additional validation in etiologically relevant models is advisable given the limitations of the NTR-MTZ model.
source: Given these limitations, it is advisable that additional validation in etiologically relevant models as we have done in this study are to be carried out.
evidence: Recommendation based on model limitations

claim: The unbiased small molecule screen together with cross-species validations has revealed that inhibition of RAAS signaling is significantly neuroprotective for DA neurons in animal PD models and human PD patients.
source: Our unbiased small molecule screen together with cross-species validations has revealed that inhibition of RAAS signaling is significantly neuroprotective for DA neurons in the context of animal PD models and moreover human PD patients.
evidence: Summary of key findings across all experiments

claim: The chemically induced Gaucher disease model presents advantages over the genetic model including significant DA neuronal loss at larval stages.
source: This chemically induced GD model presents several advantages over the genetic model of GD (Keatinge, 2015): First, it shows significant DA neuronal loss at larval stages, whereas the genetic GD model only exhibit weak and variable deficit of DA neurons at adult stages.
evidence: Comparison of model characteristics with citation to Keatinge, 2015

claim: The chemically induced Gaucher disease model can be conveniently combined with transgenic lines that label DA neurons.
source: Second, it can be conveniently combined with transgenic lines that label DA neurons.
evidence: Stated as advantage of the chemical model

claim: The conditional nature of the chemically induced Gaucher disease model allows temporal control over access to DA neurons prior to degeneration.
source: Its conditional nature further allows us to gain temporal control over the access of DA neurons prior to degeneration.
evidence: Stated as advantage of the chemical model

claim: The finding that RAAS inhibitors are neuroprotective in the Drosophila pink1-deficient model suggests that the underlying neuroprotective mechanisms are deeply conserved across evolution.
source: The finding that RAAS inhibitors are also neuroprotective in the Drosophila pink1-deficient model suggests that the underlying neuroprotective mechanisms are deeply conserved across evolution.
evidence: Inference based on conservation of neuroprotective effects across species

claim: Literature reports suggest RAAS inhibitors have neuroprotective effects in various animal models of neurodegeneration, but the mechanisms were not well characterized.
source: Intriguingly, literature search has uncovered reports of RAAS inhibitors' neuroprotective effects in various animal models of neurodegeneration, but the mechanisms were not well characterized in these studies (Grammatopoulos, 2007; Muñoz, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Grammatopoulos, 2007; Muñoz, 2006

claim: The study's findings corroborate with previous reports of RAAS inhibitors' neuroprotective effects and further demystify their actions.
source: Our findings corroborate with these reports and further demystify the actions of RAAS inhibitors, by showing that agtr1a and 1b act cell autonomously in DA neurons beyond their conventional actions on the vasculature systems.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental findings in context of prior literature

claim: Agtr1a and 1b act cell autonomously in DA neurons beyond their conventional actions on the vasculature systems.
source: Our findings corroborate with these reports and further demystify the actions of RAAS inhibitors, by showing that agtr1a and 1b act cell autonomously in DA neurons beyond their conventional actions on the vasculature systems.
evidence: Conclusion based on conditional CRISPR and morpholino experiments

claim: The upregulation of electron transport chain gene expression could be a compensatory response to mitochondrial damage or dysfunction.
source: Although upregulation of electron transport chain gene expression could be a compensatory response to mitochondrial damage or dysfunction, it could also lead to dysregulated metabolic pathways resulting in neurodegeneration (Area-Gomez et al., 2019).
evidence: Speculation about possible mechanisms with citation to Area-Gomez et al., 2019

claim: Upregulation of electron transport chain gene expression could lead to dysregulated metabolic pathways resulting in neurodegeneration.
source: Although upregulation of electron transport chain gene expression could be a compensatory response to mitochondrial damage or dysfunction, it could also lead to dysregulated metabolic pathways resulting in neurodegeneration (Area-Gomez et al., 2019).

claim: AGTR1 expression is detected in the mitochondria of a variety of cell types including DA neurons.
source: Second, AGTR1 expression is detected in the mitochondria of a variety of cell types including DA neurons (Valenzuela, 2016; Abadir, 2011), lending support that it may have a direct role in regulating mitochondrial function.
evidence: Supported by citations to Valenzuela, 2016; Abadir, 2011

claim: AGTR1 is reported to promote reactive oxygen species production and activate MAP kinase pathway leading to activation of transcription factors including NF-kB, AP-1, and P53 in vascular senescence.
source: Indeed, AGTR1 is reported to promote reactive oxygen species production and activate MAP kinase pathway that leads to the activation of transcription factors including NF-kB and AP-1, and P53 in the context of vascular senescence (Min et al., 2009).

claim: Significant upregulation of AP-1 was observed in both neurotoxic models.
source: Intriguingly, significant upregulation of AP-1 was observed in both neurotoxic models, suggesting the following possible model: Neurotoxic insults activate AGTR1, which activates kinase signaling cascades that upregulate the expression of transcription factors such as AP-1, in turn increasing the expression of mitochondrial electron transport chain genes.

claim: A possible model is that neurotoxic insults activate AGTR1, which activates kinase signaling cascades that upregulate transcription factors such as AP-1, increasing mitochondrial electron transport chain gene expression, leading to increased ROS production, mitochondrial dysfunction, and neuronal death.
source: Intriguingly, significant upregulation of AP-1 was observed in both neurotoxic models, suggesting the following possible model: Neurotoxic insults activate AGTR1, which activates kinase signaling cascades that upregulate the expression of transcription factors such as AP-1, in turn increasing the expression of mitochondrial electron transport chain genes. Such altered mitochondrial gene expression is associated with increased reactive oxygen species production leading to mitochondrial dysfunction and neuronal death.
evidence: Proposed mechanistic model based on integration of experimental findings and literature

source: RAAS pathway components are broadly expressed in the CNS, suggesting that its inhibition could be broadly neuroprotective, not only for PD, but also for other neurodegenerative diseases.

claim: RAAS inhibition could be broadly neuroprotective, not only for PD, but also for other neurodegenerative diseases.
source: RAAS pathway components are broadly expressed in the CNS, suggesting that its inhibition could be broadly neuroprotective, not only for PD, but also for other neurodegenerative diseases.
